paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: how you treat people is part of how you teach about God. Paul says elders who lead effectively are "worthy of double honor," and he backs it up with "The worker is worthy of his wages." (1 Timothy 5:17-18) Then he says to honor masters so "God's name and our teaching will not be discredited." (1 Timothy 6:1) Honor isn't just manners. People are watching, and the way you treat folks says something about the God you follow.

Paul also wants fairness, and he means it all the way down. He tells Timothy to "maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality." (1 Timothy 5:21) That means no easy pass for the people you like and no piling on the people you don't. An accusation against an elder needs "two or three witnesses," and those who persist in sin get rebuked, not ignored. (1 Timothy 5:19-20)

And here's the good news. Paul says good deeds are obvious, "and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden." (1 Timothy 5:25) I spent years in the back of a junk drawer thinking nobody noticed me, so that line hits me right in the apron. So serve well, honor well, and stay fair, baker. Even when nobody's clapping, it counts.
